<reflection>
After two experiments, the fitting results show a clear top cluster of mechanisms involving deactivation: M16, M11, M10, M9, M15, M20, M14 (NLL around -43 to -42.9). The other mechanisms have significantly higher NLL, making them less plausible. The aim for this turn is to discriminate within the top cluster by testing whether deactivation is substrate-dependent or substrate-independent. The proposed experiment uses low substrate concentration (0.1 M) relative to catalyst (0.1 M) to amplify differences: mechanisms with substrate-independent deactivation (e.g., M9) should show incomplete conversion due to catalyst deactivation during slow turnover, while mechanisms where deactivation requires substrate (e.g., M11, M14, M16) should show nearly complete conversion because deactivation is minimal at low [S].
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
The key mechanistic difference among the top candidates is the dependence of deactivation on substrate. M9 features first-order deactivation of free catalyst (cat→inactive_cat), independent of substrate. In contrast, M11, M14, and M16 involve deactivation steps that require substrate (S+cat→inactive_catS, catS→inactive_catS, S+catS→inactive_catS2). At low substrate concentration (0.1 M) with equal catalyst concentration (0.1 M), the reaction will be slow due to substrate limitation. For M9, catalyst deactivates at a rate proportional to [cat], which remains relatively high, leading to significant loss of active catalyst before all substrate is converted, resulting in incomplete conversion. For M11, M14, and M16, deactivation rates are proportional to [S] or [catS], which are low, so deactivation is minimal and substrate is fully converted. M20 combines both types of deactivation, so it may show intermediate incomplete conversion. Thus, the final product concentration will discriminate: near-complete conversion (≈0.1 M) supports substrate-dependent deactivation; significantly lower conversion supports substrate-independent deactivation.
</hypothesis>
